newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac tackles youth unemployment in packaged show.
newsitem.headline: Chirac tackles youth unemployment in packaged show.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac strives on Monday to boost the morale of young people, plagued by 25 percent unemployment, in a televised interview overshadowed by a furore over car-maker Renault's layoffs.

The Gaullist president's image-doctors, anxious to fan a slight pickup in his low popularity, have picked the futuristic Cite des Sciences in northern Paris as a backdrop for a live broadcast designed to push "a go-getting, mobilising message".

"The aim is to highlight the president's ambition to move French society forward, to emphasise the importance of movement. It's a step in his crusade for jobs for the young," a Chirac aide said of the interview (eds:1940 GMT) before an audience of young people, teachers, trainers and company heads.

Chirac had drawn widespread criticism at a previous television appearance in December for denouncing what he called a French refusal to change. Since then, he has shifted his stance to stress French people's "dynamism".
This time, Chirac will "speak of the future, of confidence, of hope" for jobs for the young, an issue he has made the priority of his seven-year term, the aide said.

In recent months, Chirac has criss-crossed the country to visit job initiatives for the young. To help prepare for the interview, he met company bosses from across France on Thursday to discuss training and apprenticeships.

Chirac aides said he would insist that despite difficulties certain schemes do work and that he would make some concrete proposals although this was not the programme's chief purpose. Twenty-five percent of 18-25 year-olds are unemployed.

In a rare protest, journalists at state-owned France-2 television have accused it of giving Chirac's team too much say over the programme, and of choosing relatively-inexperienced reporters for features on schooling, the family, companies and immigrants.

But weighing on Chirac will be Renault's closure of the large Belgian plan of Vilvoorde with the loss of 3,100 jobs, which has sparked brief strikes in several European countries and prompted protests from within all French political parties.
Six French and Belgian trade unions have called a new demonstration for Tuesday at Renault's headquarters in Boulogne-Billancourt just outside Paris.

More labour protests are also due this week in the hospital sector, with unions fighting layoffs decreed by the centre-right government's welfare reforms. Unions have put the number of job losses at 15,000-20,000.

According to an IFOP opinion poll published by the weekly Le Journal du Dimanche, only 13 percent of 14-25 year-olds count on Chirac above anyone else to prepare their future and that of French society.
Sixty-five percent of the 807 people questioned on March 5-6 said their future was up to them.

With a general election due early next year, the Socialist Party, France's biggest opposition force, is struggling to forge pacts with other leftist groups to build a credible alternative to the centre-right.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, at a congress of the small Radical Socialist Party, urged Communists and Greens to stop harping over what they agreed about and to start tackling issues which divided the Left, including the European single currency.
Socialist ex-prime minister Laurent Fabius told a radio interviewer on Sunday that victory was possible but nothing was certain yet.

"There has however been one constant for the past 20 years or more -- all outgoing governments lose elections because, as we are in a period of great economic and social difficulty, people spontaneously vote against," he said.
